captions.text: Imagine an aerospace manufacturing cell.
A new inspection task is ready.
The robot, the operator, and the part are here.
The team preparing the change may be somewhere else.
So here is the question I care about.
When that connection disappears, who owns the next move?
This is EVY and AERIS.
We are exploring how a capability can travel from a central system to an edge
cell, while control stays local.
The aircraft structure is an illustration.
Our executable robot is a simulator.
But the transfer, the interruption, and the recovery are things we can
actually challenge.
Start with what travels. In this proof, it is a signed recipe: a bounded set
of joint goals, with an exact identity and an approved target.
We are not downloading a new robot driver or asking a language model to invent
a movement. The central system offers a capability.
The edge decides whether those exact bytes are approved, compatible, current,
and allowed to run. That is the useful boundary.
We can change the task without giving the remote system the keys to local
execution. Training can become another source of a capability later.
It is not the point of this demonstration.
Now follow that same recipe.
The operator chooses an approved task.
EVY binds the action to its destination and release.
The edge inbox accepts the request.
Rust checks the signature, local approval, compatibility, expiry, and
sequence. Only an idle executor can activate it.
The task then pins its release before the local controller begins.
Notice where the network ends.
It is a delivery path, not the controller loop.
And notice what remains: durable state, committed samples, and a receipt
tied to this task. Those details let us explain what happened instead of
asking the audience to trust an animation.
Let us make the connection fail.
First, the task must be running with committed progress.
Then we cut the central data plane.
In the retained simulator proof, local work continues and completes.
A separate management observer can still read the edge.
That distinction matters: this is not a total network blackout, and it is not
a safety stop. Reconnect, ask for the same action again, and inspect the
result. A retry should return the existing receipt, not quietly start another
movement. These pictures replay retained evidence.
For a new run, the workbench gives you the actual controls and observations.
A lost connection is one trial.
An interrupted executor is another.
If that process dies, we should not paint the task green.
Durable state preserves the uncertainty.
A new action is refused until the operator explicitly recovers the executor.
Recovery records the orphaned task as interrupted.
It does not resume motion.
Another execution needs a deliberately new action.
That is less magical, and much more useful.
We can inspect the refusal, the recovery, and the new receipt.
The same discipline applies to the evidence: a browser export is an
observation. A complete captured trace still needs its independent audit.
Now pull back. Inspection positioning and rework positioning already share
this process. The next module could support another manufacturing task, but a
different robot still needs a reviewed adapter and its own acceptance.
That is the repeatable part: the contract, the delivery, local ownership,
explicit recovery, and evidence. Intel compute and Red Hat
platforms are the target foundation.
The retained separate-host baseline used Intel workers with RHEL on OpenShift.
New hardware must earn its own result.
We are not claiming an accelerator benefit, a production fleet, or physical
robot qualification just because the diagram looks convincing.
So what is the next useful decision?
Pick one cell, one approved capability, and named central and edge
hardware. Give your testing agent the repository.
It can explain the architecture, check prerequisites, collect the hardware
facts, and follow the acceptance workflow.
Then measure the things the business actually needs: rollout effort, recovery
behavior, and whether the task delivers its intended result.
The dashboard, workbench, and evidence come with the handoff.
Physical motion and real-time behavior remain separate gates.
I am Kersh. I work at Red Hat; these are my personal views.
Capability travels. Control stays. What would you
test first?
